tier_reason: First-party README table with public benchmark code (src/c/inference.c benchmark(), src/python/benchmark.py), Makefile flags (gcc -O2) and the hardware (Apple M1) named, but no compiler version, and the C and Python sides use different timers. The gain is over 50x against a Python-dispatch baseline, so it is capped at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: Iris (4-8-3), batch 1, 1M iterations: pure C 2,732,240 predictions/s (0.366 s) vs PyTorch from a single-threaded Python loop 10,596 predictions/s (94.374 s), stated as 258x; the README warns this measures Python plus PyTorch dispatch overhead, not compute throughput. MNIST (784-128-10), 100K iterations: pure C 4,244 predictions/s (23.563 s) vs PyTorch 22,502 (0.444 s), i.e. PyTorch about 5.3x faster (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Educational project with 0 stars. The 258x win is Python-interpreter and PyTorch dispatch overhead on a 4-feature input (the README says so), not a like-for-like library comparison: the PyTorch side is a Python loop that calls .item() on every prediction and is timed with time.time() (wall clock), while the C side is timed with clock() (CPU time) and is not compared against libtorch or any C/C++ inference engine. The C predict() mallocs and frees two buffers per call and uses naive loops with no SIMD, so on the compute-bound MNIST case PyTorch wins by about 5x. Single Apple M1 run, compiler version unstated.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly. Metadata confirmed (MIT, 0 stars, last commit 2026-03-25, active). Keep only as a flagged toy: its single win is overhead-bound and it loses on the compute-bound workload.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D. The project's launch blog post (source in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer-ai.github.io) gives kernel-level numbers against vLLM 0.2.6 PageAttention and FlashAttention 2.4.2 (NVCC from CUDA 12.3.1, nvbench cold-L2 timing, H100/A100/RTX 6000 Ada/RTX 4090). The peer-reviewed MLSys 2025 paper (proceedings.mlsys.org listing seen in search results; the PDF was blocked here) reports serving-latency wins over compiler (Triton) backends. Build flags and an exact benchmark code path for the published figures are not stated, so not A.

corrections.baseline: vLLM 0.2.6 PageAttention kernels and FlashAttention 2.4.2 (kernel-level, 2024 launch blog); Triton-based compiler attention backends in LLM serving (MLSys 2025 paper)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Launch blog 'Accelerating Self-Attentions for LLM Serving with FlashInfer' (2024-02-02, FlashInfer 0.0.1): cascade inference gives 'up to 31x speedup compared to the baseline vLLM PageAttention implementation' for shared-prefix batch decoding (32768-token shared prompt, batch size >=128, unique KV length <=256, H100 SXM 80GB) and 26x over FlashInfer's own non-cascaded batch decode; 'up to 2-3x speedup for Grouped-Query Attention on A100 & H100, compared to vLLM implementation'; batch GQA decode with Tensor Cores '3x faster than vLLM PagaAttention when batch_size=64'; prefill and decode kernels described as best on all 4 GPUs against FlashAttention 2.4.2 (plots only). MLSys 2025 paper abstract (seen via a search result; paper blocked here): 29-69% inter-token-latency reduction compared to compiler backends on an LLM serving benchmark, 28-30% latency reduction for long-context inference, 13-17% speedup for LLM serving with parallel generation.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: NVCC from CUDA 12.3.1 for FlashInfer and FlashAttention (built from source); vLLM 0.2.6 from prebuilt pip wheels; build flags not stated; kernels timed with NVIDIA nvbench, cold L2
corrections.hardware: H100 SXM 80GB, A100 PCIe 80GB, RTX 6000 Ada, RTX 4090 (2024 launch blog)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 6.5k stars, 1.5k forks; used by vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, MLC-LLM; PyPI flashinfer-python 0.7.0.post1 uploaded 2026-09-29
corrections.caveats: The quoted kernel numbers are first-party and from 2024 (FlashInfer 0.0.1 against FlashAttention 2.4.2 and vLLM 0.2.6); nobody has re-published them for current versions. The 31x figure is a best-case corner (very long shared prefix, large batch) against a vLLM kernel that did not optimize shared prefixes. Today FlashInfer also dispatches to FlashAttention-2/3, cuDNN, CUTLASS and TensorRT-LLM backends, so part of its current speed comes from third-party kernels, and its benchmarks/flashinfer_benchmark.py only prints per-backend timings (in the README's sample B200 ragged-prefill run the cuDNN backend beat fa2 and cutlass). The MLSys 2025 paper and the flashinfer.ai blog were blocked here; the paper's numbers come from a search-result abstract. Build flags for the published runs are not stated.
